title: Listening in Nat Narain
hookLine: a lively raga for a slow listen

lines: A LIVELY RAGA, LISTENED TO SLOWLY.
cards: Speed hides things. A fast song comes on in the car, and the first time through, you catch the beat and not much else.
Somewhere around the third play, a line you'd been half-singing comes clear, and it isn't what you thought. Speed is wonderful, and it still hides things.
So today, something slightly odd: one hymn from a lively raga, listened to slowly.

teach.h: I LAY NO COMPLAINT AGAINST ANYONE.
teach.b: This Nat Narain hymn is by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, and in plain English, not word for word, it opens: I lay no complaint against anyone; whatever you have done is sweet to my mind.
Heard quickly, over a bright tune, that can slip past as a pleasant line. Heard slowly, it asks a great deal. No complaint against anyone.
Not the coworker, not the relative, not the delayed train. The hymn isn't claiming nothing hard ever happens.

teach.h: WHAT YOU DO IS SWEET TO MY MIND.
teach.b: It describes a person who has stopped keeping a file of grievances, because what comes is received as the Creator's doing and tasted as sweet. Guru Arjan sings the same thought in Raga Asa: what you do seems sweet to me.
Sikhs speak of this as living within hukam, the divine order, and taking it as sweet. That's a big idea to hear at speed.
So the practice this path gives for Nat Narain is to listen twice: once letting the music lift you along, then again following the words, line by line. The two listens don't compete.
Kirtan holds the liveliness and the depth at once; a listener sometimes needs two passes to catch up. Slowing down isn't correcting the raga.
It's letting the words land after the music has opened the door.
That's today's line: slow the lively.

how: Sikhs listen to kirtan in the gurdwara, at home and through recordings, and many follow along with the words of the Guru Granth Sahib, often with a translation on a screen or in a book, so the music and the meaning arrive together.

games.q: what does “listening in nat narain” mean?
o: humming the tune only, since the words are too hard to follow
playing the lively hymns faster so the mind can't drift off
hearing a lively hymn twice: once for the tune, once for the words

games.q: what's inside the listen — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Arjan's hymn claims nothing hard ever happens
it describes someone who receives what comes as the Creator's doing, without a file of grievances.
Guru Arjan sings a similar thought in Raga Asa
what you do seems sweet to me: the same idea in another raga.
slowing down a lively raga means correcting it
the liveliness is real; the slow listen just lets the words land too.

games.q: a friend plays you a lively shabad. the tune is great, and you have no idea what it said. what does this path suggest?
o: skip the music and only read it.
listen twice: once for the music, once for the words.
ask them to play it at half speed.
games.why: the practice for this raga is to listen twice: let the music lift you, then follow the words. neither listen cancels the other.

practice: Sit comfortably and bring to mind one small complaint from this week, the kind that replays on its own, and just let it be there.
Then set Guru Arjan's line beside it, no complaint against anyone, without arguing and without forcing an answer, and breathe with the two side by side.
If you pray, say Waheguru slowly on the out-breath; if you don't, simply keep breathing.

wordCard.voice: Listening in Nat Narain. Hearing a lively raga twice: once for the music, once for words like Guru Arjan's, I lay no complaint against anyone. Today's word.

orig.note: a complaint, a reproach: the word Guru Arjan sets aside in his Nat Narain hymn.

carryVoice: Your line: slow the lively. Some lines only open up on the second pass. I'll be here tomorrow.
